Dear Secretary Reese: 
 
Pursuant to Section 205 of the Federal Power Act1 and the August 14, 2026 letter order 
issued in Docket No. EL26-67-000,2 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) hereby submits 
revisions to the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”)3 to establish disturbance ride-
through requirements applicable to Eligible Customers taking transmission service on behalf of 
Large Computational Loads, a targeted subset of Large Loads4 that may pose heightened 
operational risks to the Bulk Electric System and PJM Transmission System during grid

The proposed Tariff revisions mitigate threats to the reliability of the Transmission System 
and Bulk Electric System posed by Eligible Customers taking transmission service on behalf of 
Large Computational Loads by:     
(1) defining Large Computational Loads, a subset of Large Loads that may pose 
heightened operational risks in the PJM Region, and thus trigger operational 
requirements on Eligible Customers serving them;  
(2) setting the framework for minimum voltage ride-through and frequency ride-through 
requirements with which Eligible Customers taking transmission service on behalf of 
Large Computational Load must comply, which establishes the necessary groundwork 
for more detailed ride-through standards to be promulgated through revisions to PJM’s 
Manuals; and 
(3) setting a framework for other operational requirements to be established in the 
Manuals, with which Eligible Customers taking transmission service on behalf of Large 
Computational Load must comply, relating to:  ramp rate requirements, 
electromagnetic transient performance requirements, operation, coordination, and 
maintenance of necessary auxiliary equipment, control technologies and protection 
systems,

The proposed Tariff provisions setting forth ride-through and other operational 
requirements state that these requirements on Eligible Customers taking transmission service on 
behalf of Large Computational Loads shall be set forth in PJM’s Manuals.9  At present, PJM is at 
an advanced stage of the process for developing Manual language for the ride-through 
requirement.  PJM plans to commence stakeholder engagement in early 2027 to develop Manual

PJM respectfully requests that the Commission accept the proposed Tariff revisions 
addressing ride-through requirements and the Tariff language establishing the framework for other 
proposed operational requirements in the Manuals, effective January 16, 2027, which is 61 days 
after the date of this filing.10   
For the reasons set forth below, the proposed revisions are just and reasonable.  However, 
if the Commission deems necessary, and to help facilitate the Commission’s acceptance of this 
filing without delay so that PJM can address the short-term needs for ride through requirements, 
PJM provides notice that it consents to the Commission’s exercise of authority to sever any 
element of the proposed Tariff language to the extent necessary and permitted under sections 205 
and 206 of the FPA and NRG Power Marketing, LLC v. FERC.11  In particular, PJM consents to 
severance of the ride-through requirements from Tariff revisions proposed herein that pertain to 
other operational requirements because, as discussed further below, recent large load transfer 
events have made it abundantly clear that PJM already faces the serious reliability concerns that

are driving the need for the ride-through requirements in the short term.  Indeed, the Manual 
language for the ride-through requirements are in an advanced stage of development. 
Lastly, PJM is also addressing the Commission’s compliance directive in the June 2026 
Co-Located Load Order requiring an annual report regarding the provision of new transmission 
services.12  PJM proposes to post on its website a report containing information about the demand 
for and use of:  Network Integration Transmission Service to the extent Interim Network 
Integration Transmission Service was also requested; Interim Network Integration Transmission 
Service; Firm Contract Demand Service; and Non-Firm Contract Demand Service, in a manner 
consistent with the method and substance of the Commission’s compliance directive.13  This 
proposed revision is just and reasonable because the annual report would give the Commission, 
states, PJM market participants, and stakeholders the benefit of additional transparency about the 
new transmission services being offered in PJM.  The Commission should accept this annual report 
proposal as just and reasonable or on compliance with the Co-Located Load Order.14     
I. 
BACKGROUND 
A. 
PJM Already Faces Risks Arising from Large Load-Transfer Events that 
Necessitate Ride-Through Requirements 
Unlike many of the other Regional Transmission Organizations and Independent System 
Operators (“RTOs/ISOs”) in the country, PJM already has approximately 10 GW of computational 
load in its footprint and, in recent years, has already experienced the reliability and operational 
impacts of large load transfer events.  For example: (1) on July 10, 2024, an approximately 1.5

gigawatt (“GW”) large load transfer event caused frequency to increase to 60.047 Hz and voltage 
to increase to 1.07 per unit (“p.u.”), (2) on February 17, 2025, an approximately 1.8 GW large load 
transfer event caused frequency to increase to 60.047 Hz and voltage to increase to 1.07 per unit 
(“p.u.”),  and (3) on July 22, 2026, an approximately 3.9 GW large load event caused frequency in 
the Eastern Interconnection to reach 60.092 Hz and voltage to increase with a peak of ~1.138 p.u.15  
As such, establishing minimum voltage ride-through and frequency ride-through requirements 
standards for Eligible Customers serving large loads is particularly critical to the reliability of the 
PJM Region.   
According to the testimony of PJM Senior Manager, Generation Modeling and Dynamics 
Studies in the Planning Division Mr. David Egan, transfer events such as the one that occurred this 
past July “demonstrate[] how large amounts of load can disconnect in a very short period of time 
in response to transmission system conditions” which “can unnecessarily introduce additional 
dynamic impacts and exacerbate the underlying disturbance.”16   
Critically, Mr. Egan explains, “[w]hen a large block of load disconnects unexpectedly, the 
actual system response may differ substantially from the conditions anticipated by planners and 
operators. Such disconnects can alter power flows, voltage profiles, frequency response, and 
system dynamics across a broad geographic area.”17  Mr. Egan further explains:  
When several thousand megawatts of load disconnect within a short period of time, 
the resulting changes in voltage, frequency, and power flows can alter the response 
of generators throughout the interconnected system. These changes can affect the 
operation of excitation systems, voltage regulators, turbine-governor controls, and

magnitude and concentration of load transfers increase, so does the potential for 
these impacts to affect the broader interconnected system and complicate the 
restoration of stable system conditions following a disturbance.18 
 
Such events pose serious threats to the reliability and safety of the Bulk Electric System in 
the PJM Region.  In this regard, the Commission’s Show Cause Order states that PJM’s Tariff 
appears to be unjust and unreasonable because it “does not specify ramp rate or ride-through 
requirements which the transmission customer taking transmission service on behalf of the large 
load must comply.”19 The Show Cause Order also recognizes the “unique nature of . . . large loads 
creates challenges for operation of the transmission system and necessitates greater visibility and 
operational control when providing transmission service to transmission customers on behalf of 
large loads, without which the reliability of the transmission system could be at risk.”20 
 
The industry is facing unprecedented load growth, driven largely by data centers. PJM’s 
load forecast predicts peak load growth of 32 GW from 2024 to 2030, 30 GW of which is 
attributable to data centers.21 PJM is expected to host as much as 70% of future U.S. data center 
development, representing highly concentrated demand, especially in northern Virginia’s “data 
center alley.”  Thus, the proposed Tariff revisions are not only directly responsive to the Show 
Cause Order but are necessary to ensure the reliability and safety of PJM’s systems.

B. 
Consultation with Stakeholders in the Development of the Proposed Tariff 
Language Regarding Large Computational Load and Ride Through 
Requirements 
The proposed Tariff language addresses concerns raised by the Commission.  First, the 
proposed Tariff revisions are directly responsive to the express, preliminary findings set forth in 
the Order to Show Cause.   
Second, the proposed definition of Large Computational Load and the Tariff revisions 
associated with ride-through requirements were presented to stakeholders during the September 8, 
2026 Planning Committee meeting.22  Concurrently, throughout the stakeholder process, PJM has 
presented stakeholders with proposed Manual language setting forth the proposed technical ride 
through performance requirements for Large Computational Loads.  
Third, on September 15, 2026, PJM held a special session of the Planning Committee 
dedicated to educating stakeholders about the impetus for the proposed ride-through requirements, 
including reliability concerns.23   
Fourth, PJM presented revised Tariff and Manual language defining Large Computational 
Load and addressing ride-through requirements during the October 6, 2026 Planning Committee 
meeting, including a comprehensive page-by-page review of the proposed provisions and

Fifth, as described further, below, and in the declaration of Mr. Egan, the proposal is

address potential gaps in processes for evaluating reliability impacts and transmission needs of 
Large Loads.  PJM has not yet commenced stakeholder discussions to develop these requirements 
although they have been acknowledged in stakeholder consultations.25 PJM has indicated that

Under these additional proposed Tariff provisions, PJM is committing to develop 
requirements in the Manuals for Eligible Customer taking transmission service on behalf of Large 
Computational Loads to comply with in order to address other operational requirements for fast-
ramping load that may impact the transmission system, as described in the Large Load Show Cause 
Order.27  The Manual language will be developed and specified in the PJM Manuals only after 
PJM has undergone the requisite additional study and stakeholder engagement in 2027.28    
II. 
THE PROPOSED TARIFF REVISIONS ARE JUST AND REASONABLE 
A. 
PJM Proposes to Define Large Computational Loads, the Relevant Subset of 
Large Loads in PJM for Purposes of the Proposed Operational Requirements  
As a preliminary matter, PJM proposes to apply the ride-through requirements for large 
loads to Eligible Customers taking transmission service on behalf of a subset of Large Loads, 
which PJM refers to as “Large Computational Load.”  PJM proposes to add a definition of Large 
Computational Load to the Tariff: 
“Large Computational Load” shall mean Large Load containing 25 MW or greater

B) Materially Modified Large Computational Load. Existing Large Load that

Large Computational Load is Large Load that “contain[s] 25 MW or greater of maximum 
load served through power electronic conversion equipment.”29  As Mr. Egan testifies, the 25 MW 
“evolved from PJM’s experience evaluating large co-located loads, stakeholder feedback on earlier 
draft language, and a review of approaches being developed by other regions, particularly 
MISO.”30  Furthermore, as Mr. Egan testifies, PJM tied the definition of Large Computational 
Load to a threshold quantity of “power electronic conversation equipment” because: 
PJM observed through its co-location and large load analyses that Large 
Computational Load facilities generally consist of two primary categories of load: 
(1) cooling and support infrastructure loads used to remove heat and maintain 
facility operation, and (2) electronics-based loads supplied through power 
 
29 Tariff, Part I, Definitions L–M–N (Large Computational Load).

electronic conversion equipment, including the AC-to-DC systems that serve 
information technology equipment and similar technologies. The reliability 
concern underlying PJM’s proposed requirements is primarily associated with the 
electronics-based portion of the load, as these systems can rapidly alter their 
demand or transfer off the Bulk Electric System during disturbance conditions. 
While the proportion of facility load attributable to cooling versus electronics varies 
across facility vintages and designs, PJM concluded that the defining reliability 
characteristic is the presence of substantial power electronic conversion equipment 
rather than the specific end use served by that equipment.31 
 
The targeted application of ride-through requirements to Large Loads that meet the Large 
Computational Load definition is just and reasonable.  First, the proposed definition recognizes 
that ride-through and other operational requirements being developed are intended to apply only 
to Eligible Customers serving Large Loads with operating characteristics warranting additional 
reliability consideration.  Thus, for purposes of managing operational risk, defining Large 
Computational Load supports a more targeted approach than applying the same ride-through and 
other operational requirements to all Eligible Customers serving Large Loads without regard to 
facility type or operating behavior.   
Second, the proposed definition of Large Computational Load is aligned with NERC’s 
proposed definition of computational load entities, which has likewise recognized that 
computational loads may warrant reliability requirements distinct from those applicable to 
traditional loads.32  Both PJM’s proposed definition of Large Computational Load and NERC’s 
developing definition recognize that power electronic conversion equipment that serves 
information technology, such as servers, storage, and networking hardware, similarly focus on the

industry or customer type.  As Mr. Egan explains, PJM’s definition of Large Computational Load 
is tailored to the specific needs of the PJM Region, while NERC’s developing definition of 
computational load, along with relevant registration criteria and Reliability Standards, is intended 
to determine which Large Loads will be subject to NERC’s mandatory reliability requirements.  
Specifically, “PJM concluded that the relevant reliability characteristic” of Large Loads in PJM 
“is not limited to servers or computational facilities, but rather the presence of large quantities of 
power electronic conversion equipment capable of exhibiting similar disturbance-response 
characteristics.”33 Defining Large Computational Loads as Large Loads meeting a threshold 
quantity of power electronic conversion equipment, “encompasses data centers” within the 
definition of Large Computational Load “while also remaining applicable to other emerging load 
types that rely heavily on power-electronic conversion technologies, such as certain hydrogen 
production facilities and other future industrial processes.”34 
Third, the differences in PJM’s definition of Large Computational Load and NERC’s 
developing definition reflect the different purposes and responsibilities of PJM and NERC.  
Indeed, as described further, below, the proposed Tariff language establishing ride-through 
requirements for Large Computational Load allows an Eligible Customer or Transmission Owner 
to modify its ride-through requirements “to address changes in system conditions, reliability needs, 
applicable NERC Reliability Standards or Transmission Provider operating requirements, 
provided such requirements continue to meet or exceed the minimum requirements established by

Fourth, PJM’s proposed approach to defining a specific subset of Large Load reflects 
PJM’s review and evaluation of emerging large-load and computational-load definitions under 
development by industry organizations and transmission providers.36 These industry efforts reflect 
a common recognition that certain computational loads present reliability considerations that differ 
from those associated with traditional commercial and industrial loads.  PJM’s proposed definition 
is generally consistent with the applicability thresholds being adopted or proposed elsewhere in 
the industry.  For example, MISO has similarly identified a subset of large load as computational 
load to which its proposed ride-through requirements will apply.  MISO has also similarly 
proposed to define computational load as “Large Load comprised of 25 MW or more of Demand 
from information technology equipment, such as servers, storage, and network hardware.”37  
Although specific criteria vary across regions, these frameworks reflect a common 
recognition that large computational facilities can present unique reliability considerations 
requiring enhanced planning, modeling, and operational oversight.  Consistent with these industry 
developments, PJM’s proposed Large Computational Load definition identifies facilities 
containing substantial computational load that may create material reliability impacts if they 
respond to transmission disturbances in a coordinated manner. PJM’s proposed criteria are 
informed by these industry efforts but were ultimately developed based on PJM’s own reliability 
assessments, operational experience, planning studies, and analyses of Large Computation Load

PJM is proposing to revise its Tariff to establish a framework for setting minimum voltage 
and frequency ride-through requirements, with which Eligible Customers taking transmission 
service on behalf of both existing and new Large Computational Loads must comply.39  Under the 
proposed language in Tariff, Part III, section 28.2, the Transmission Provider shall establish 
“minimum voltage ride-through and frequency ride-through requirements with which Eligible 
Customers taking transmission service on behalf of Large Computational Load must comply, 
which shall be set forth in the PJM Manuals.”  The proposed language sets a floor for disturbance 
ride-through requirements while also leaving room for Transmission Owners or Eligible 
Customers to establish ride-through requirements that are “no less stringent than the minimum 
requirements established by Transmission Provider in the PJM Manuals[]” where “the 
Transmission Owner determines that such requirements are necessary to maintain the reliability, 
security, or operational performance of its transmission facilities or the Transmission System.”40  
Furthermore, any ride-through requirements established by an Eligible Customer or Transmission 
Owner must “be based upon reliability, planning, operational, stability, protection coordination, 
voltage performance, frequency performance, restoration, balancing, reserve management or other

III. 
STAKEHOLDER ENGAGEMENT 
The proposed Tariff revisions defining Large Computational Load and establishing ride-
through requirements follow an expedited stakeholder engagement effort.  PJM presented its initial 
proposal to stakeholders at the September 8, 2026 Planning Committee meeting.66 PJM 
subsequently conducted a dedicated Planning Committee education session on September 15, 
2026, during which Planning and Operations subject matter experts presented the July 22, 2026 
load transfer event, the associated reliability concerns, and the technical basis supporting the 
proposed ride-through requirements.67  PJM then presented revised Tariff and Manual language at 
the October 6, 2026 Planning Committee meeting.68 
With respect to other ongoing operational requirements applicable to Eligible Customers 
taking transmission on behalf of Large Computational Load, PJM is committed to developing 
Manual language through the stakeholder process starting in early 2027.  PJM has in other fora 
and in posted materials – particularly at and for the Co-Located Load Workshops, the Markets and 
Reliability Committee, and the Special Members Committee convened on November 5, 2026 
preceding this Section 205 filing – noted the operational requirements described in the Show Cause 
Order.
